clinical: Myocardial infarction and troponin

Occlusion of an epicardial coronary artery by thrombus on a ruptured plaque kills cardiomyocytes from the subendocardium outwards (the wavefront). Damaged cells leak cardiac troponin I and T, which rise within about 3 hours and stay raised for 1-2 weeks. Under the microscope: wavy fibres and contraction bands in the first hours, coagulative necrosis with neutrophils at 1-3 days, macrophages at 3-7 days (when the wall is weakest and rupture is most likely), granulation tissue at 1-2 weeks and a collagen scar by about 2 months. Adult cardiomyocytes renew only about 1% a year at age 25 and less later, so the loss is repaired with scar, not new muscle.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Autosomal dominant mutations in sarcomere genes (beta-myosin heavy chain, myosin-binding protein C, troponin T) cause asymmetric septal hypertrophy with myocyte disarray: fibres and myofibrils lie in a whorled, haphazard pattern instead of the parallel alignment seen here, with interstitial fibrosis. The disarray is an arrhythmic substrate and a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.
Hypertrophy, dilatation and the capillary supply

Pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) adds sarcomeres in parallel, so cells widen and the wall thickens (concentric hypertrophy), with large rectangular 'boxcar' nuclei. Volume overload adds them in series, so cells lengthen and the chamber dilates (eccentric hypertrophy). Capillary growth does not keep pace with the larger cells, so the diffusion distance grows; and since the heart already extracts about 70-75% of the oxygen delivered, it can meet extra demand only by increasing flow, so the subendocardium of a hypertrophied ventricle is prone to ischaemia.
Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and myocarditis

Mutations in desmosomal proteins of the intercalated disc (plakophilin-2 is the commonest; also desmoplakin, desmoglein-2, desmocollin-2 and plakoglobin) let cells pull apart under stretch. The lost muscle is replaced by fat and fibrous tissue, mainly in the right ventricle, giving ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death in the young. Naxos disease, from a plakoglobin mutation, adds woolly hair and thickened palms and soles because the same proteins hold skin cells together. In viral myocarditis (coxsackie B and others) lymphocytes surround and destroy individual cardiomyocytes.
Gap junctions, conduction and re-entry

Gap junctions couple the cells electrically, so the impulse spreads through the ventricle as one wave; anything that slows or uncouples them favours re-entry circuits. Acute ischaemia (acidosis, raised intracellular calcium) closes the channels. In chronic ischaemia and heart failure connexin-43 is lost from the discs and redistributed along the sides of the cells, so conduction becomes slow and disorganised; the surviving muscle at the edge of an old infarct is the typical source of ventricular tachycardia.

clinical: Myocardial infarction territories and coronary dominance

Each coronary branch supplies a predictable territory, so the leads with ST elevation point to the culprit. Anterior interventricular artery (LAD): anterior wall, apex and the anterior two-thirds of the septum, leads V1-V4; an occlusion before the first septal perforator can also injure the bundle branches. Circumflex and its obtuse marginal branches: lateral wall, leads I, aVL, V5-V6 (an isolated circumflex occlusion is often quiet on the ECG). Right coronary artery: about 70-80% of hearts are right-dominant, as this model is, so the RCA supplies the inferior wall through the posterior interventricular artery (leads II, III, aVF) and the posterior wall through the posterolateral branches (ST depression in V1-V3), plus the right ventricle (ST elevation in V4R, hypotension that worsens with nitrates) and usually the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodal arteries, hence bradycardia and heart block. About 10% of hearts are left-dominant: the circumflex then reaches the crux and an inferior infarct is a circumflex event.
Valve disease and auscultation areas

Valves are heard downstream of where they lie: aortic, right 2nd intercostal space at the sternal edge; pulmonary, left 2nd space; tricuspid, left lower sternal border; mitral, the apex (left 5th space, midclavicular line). S1 is closure of the atrioventricular valves, S2 of the semilunar valves (A2 then P2, splitting more on inspiration). Aortic stenosis: ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids (calcific degeneration, or a congenitally bicuspid valve). Mitral regurgitation: pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Mitral stenosis (rheumatic, with fused commissures and shortened chordae): mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap, left atrial enlargement and atrial fibrillation. Aortic regurgitation: early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a collapsing pulse. Tricuspid regurgitation: pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration, with large v waves in the jugular pulse, usually from a dilated right ventricle stretching the annulus.
Papillary muscles, chordae and mitral regurgitation

Papillary muscles do not open or close a valve; they tether the leaflets through the chordae so the leaflets are not blown back into the atrium when the ventricle contracts. The anterolateral papillary muscle has a double blood supply (diagonal branches of the LAD and obtuse marginal branches of the circumflex); the posteromedial muscle has a single one (the posterior interventricular artery, from the RCA in right-dominant hearts), so it is the one that ruptures, 2-7 days after an inferior infarct, causing acute severe mitral regurgitation with pulmonary oedema and shock. Ruptured chordae also occur in myxomatous mitral valve prolapse (mid-systolic click, late systolic murmur) and infective endocarditis. A dilated ventricle pulls the papillary muscles apart and tethers the leaflets, giving functional mitral regurgitation.
Atrial fibrillation, the left auricle and the pulmonary veins

Most triggers of atrial fibrillation fire from muscle sleeves that extend into the pulmonary veins, so catheter ablation isolates the four pulmonary vein openings in the back wall of the left atrium. In non-valvular atrial fibrillation about 90% of left atrial thrombi form in the left auricle, a narrow pouch whose blood stagnates; embolism to the brain causes stroke, which is why patients are anticoagulated or the auricle is occluded. The circumflex artery and great cardiac vein run beside the base of the auricle, and the oesophagus lies directly behind the left atrium's posterior wall (atrio-oesophageal fistula is a rare, lethal complication of ablation).
Cardiac veins and the coronary sinus in practice

Most cardiac venous blood returns through the great, middle and small cardiac veins to the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium beside the inferior vena cava; the anterior cardiac veins drain directly into the atrium. Left ventricular leads for cardiac resynchronisation therapy are passed through the coronary sinus opening (which may be guarded by a Thebesian valve) into a lateral or posterior tributary, such as the left marginal vein or the posterior vein of the left ventricle. Retrograde cardioplegia is delivered by a balloon catheter in the coronary sinus. A dilated coronary sinus points to raised right atrial pressure or a persistent left superior vena cava, which drains into it; the oblique vein of the left atrium is that vessel's remnant.
Septal defects and fetal remnants

The interatrial septum carries the fossa ovalis, the remnant of the foramen ovale. A patent foramen ovale persists in about a quarter of adults and can let a venous clot cross to the systemic circulation (paradoxical embolism). Atrial septal defects (secundum, in the fossa ovalis, is the commonest) load the right heart and give a fixed split S2. Most ventricular septal defects lie in the small membranous part of the interventricular septum below the aortic valve, beside the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve, and give a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; a large left-to-right shunt can reverse as pulmonary vascular resistance rises (Eisenmenger syndrome).

clinical: Nephrotic and nephritic syndromes

Injury to the podocytes and glomerular basement membrane leaks protein. Nephrotic syndrome (more than 3.5 g of protein a day, low albumin, oedema, high cholesterol, infections and thrombosis) occurs in minimal change disease (foot-process effacement seen only by electron microscopy, steroid-responsive, commonest in children), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy and diabetic nephropathy (thickened basement membrane, mesangial nodules). Inflammation of the glomerular capillaries causes nephritic syndrome: haematuria with red-cell casts, hypertension, oliguria and a rising creatinine, as in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy (IgA deposited in the mesangium). In Alport syndrome a type IV collagen defect splits the basement membrane: haematuria, deafness and eye changes.
Diuretic targets along the nephron

Each class blocks one transporter. Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase) and SGLT2 inhibitors act on the proximal convoluted tubule. Loop diuretics such as furosemide block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, the most powerful because about a quarter of the filtered sodium is reabsorbed there; they also waste calcium, since the lumen-positive potential that drives its reabsorption is lost. Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule and retain calcium. Amiloride (ENaC) and spironolactone or eplerenone (the mineralocorticoid receptor) act on the principal cells of the connecting tubule and collecting duct, sparing potassium. Vasopressin V2 antagonists such as tolvaptan block the insertion of aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct.
Acute tubular necrosis

Ischaemia (shock, sepsis) or toxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, cisplatin) kill tubular cells, above all in the proximal straight tubule and thick ascending limb, which work hard and lie in the poorly oxygenated outer medulla. Dead cells slough into the lumen and form muddy-brown granular casts. Urine sodium is high (fractional excretion above 2%) and the urine cannot be concentrated; the patient is oliguric for days to weeks until the tubular epithelium regenerates, often followed by a polyuric recovery phase.
Renin, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs

Filtration is held up by two opposing tones: prostaglandin dilatation of the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole. The granular cells release renin when the afferent arteriole is stretched less, when the macula densa senses low NaCl and with sympathetic stimulation. ACE inhibitors and ARBs relax the efferent arteriole and NSAIDs remove the afferent dilatation; either can drop glomerular pressure and cause acute kidney injury when perfusion is already marginal (dehydration, heart failure, cirrhosis, bilateral renal artery stenosis), and an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus a diuretic plus an NSAID (the 'triple whammy') is especially risky. Renal artery stenosis, from atherosclerosis in older people or fibromuscular dysplasia in young women, raises blood pressure through renin.
Renal infarction and papillary necrosis

Segmental, interlobar and arcuate arteries are end arteries: an embolus (atrial fibrillation, endocarditis) causes a pale wedge-shaped infarct with its base on the capsule, with flank pain and haematuria. The papillae lie at the far end of the vasa recta, where the oxygen tension is lowest, so they die first (papillary necrosis) in analgesic nephropathy, diabetes, sickle cell disease and obstructive infection; a sloughed papilla can block the ureter.
Stones, hydronephrosis and pyelonephritis

Most stones are calcium oxalate, seeded on papillary (Randall) plaques. A stone lodges where the ureter narrows (the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the vesicoureteric junction) and causes loin-to-groin colic with haematuria. Obstruction dilates the pelvis and calyces (hydronephrosis: clubbed calyces, and a thin cortex if it lasts), and an infected obstructed kidney is an emergency that needs drainage. Ascending infection, usually E. coli and helped by reflux or obstruction, climbs the collecting ducts from the papillae to cause pyelonephritis: fever, loin pain, and white-cell casts in the urine.

capillary_bed.name: Capillaries and Lymphatic Capillaries

Beside it, 3 times larger: continuous, fenestrated and sinusoidal capillaries cut lengthwise.
capillary_bed.scale_note: Network to scale (capillaries 8 µm, red cells 7.5 µm); the three capillary types are 3x with fenestrae enlarged further. The ruler applies to the network only.

lymph_drainage.name: Lymphatic Trunks and Ducts
lymph_drainage.summary: Where lymph returns to the blood. The cisterna chyli collects the intestinal and lumbar trunks in front of L1-L2; the thoracic duct climbs through the aortic hiatus and the posterior mediastinum, crosses to the left and empties into the left venous angle. The short right lymphatic duct takes the right jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks to the right venous angle. Green = thoracic duct territory, teal = right lymphatic duct territory.
lymph_drainage.scale_note: Life size, 1 unit = 1 mm, built on the atlas body: the great veins, aorta, oesophagus, spine and lymph nodes are the atlas structures. The ducts and trunks are drawn at typical diameters and their courses are simplified.

duodenum.name: Duodenum Wall
duodenum.summary: A duodenal wall block: leaf-like villi covered by enterocytes and goblet cells, crypts with Paneth and stem cells, the lamina propria with lacteals and capillaries, the muscularis mucosae, a submucosa full of Brunner glands whose ducts open into the crypts, the Meissner and Auerbach plexuses, inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle, and the serosa. Brunner glands in the submucosa are what identify the duodenum.
duodenum.scale_note: Coordinates are millimetres: block 1.28 mm wide, 0.72 mm deep. Villi about 0.5 mm tall. Cell sizes, brush border and nuclei are enlarged for teaching; counts of villi, crypts and lobules are representative.

colon_wall.name: Colon Wall
colon_wall.summary: A colon wall block: a flat surface with crypt openings (no villi), straight test-tube crypts full of goblet cells with stem cells at their bases, lamina propria rich in immune cells and capillaries, a lymphoid follicle crossing the muscularis mucosae, the submucosa with vessels and Meissner's plexus, inner circular muscle, Auerbach's plexus, the outer longitudinal muscle thickened into a taenia coli, and the serosa.
colon_wall.scale_note: Tissue block in millimetres: 0.96 mm wide and 0.48 mm deep; crypts about 0.44 mm deep. The separate cell detail on the right is magnified 8 times, so the ruler applies to the tissue block only. Counts are representative.

A separate teaching set on the right repeats the islet and the exocrine units with space around them.
pancreas.scale_note: Millimetres; both regions share one scale. Counts and spacing are chosen for teaching.

neuron.name: Neuron: Cell, Node of Ranvier and Synapse
neuron.summary: A multipolar neuron: dendrites, a cell body with nucleus, nucleolus, Nissl substance (rough ER), Golgi and mitochondria, the axon hillock and initial segment, an axon wrapped in myelin with nodes of Ranvier, and axon terminals with boutons. Two enlargements: a node of Ranvier with its sodium channels, and an excitatory synapse with vesicles, active zone, calcium channels, AMPA receptors and the postsynaptic density.
neuron.scale_note: Three scales. The whole neuron is schematic (proportions chosen for clarity, axon shortened, sodium channels drawn far larger than life). The node of Ranvier enlargement is to true scale: 1 unit = 5 nm. The synapse enlargement is to true scale: 1 unit ≈ 5.9 nm (vesicles about 40 nm, cleft about 24 nm). No single ruler applies to the whole model.
